display_title: Latin American Cartels Expand Across Europe
display_title_he: קרטלים מאמריקה הלטינית מתרחבים ברחבי אירופה
short_summary: A major press investigation reveals that Latin American criminal networks now operate across Europe, driven by surging cocaine production and lucrative profit margins.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’

paragraphs: A comprehensive four-month investigation by The Guardian has exposed the dramatic expansion of Latin American organised crime across Europe. Drawing on police and intelligence databases alongside interviews with judges, prosecutors, and experts across eight nations, the inquiry confirms that syndicates from Colombia, Brazil, Mexico, Ecuador, Venezuela, and the United States maintain active operations in at least twelve European countries. This continental penetration is directly tied to soaring contraband flows, with European cocaine seizures rising by 471 percent between 2014 and 2024 as law enforcement dismantled an increasing number of local facilities refining cocaine derivatives.

The presence of Latin American syndicates in Europe is not entirely unprecedented; during the 1980s, Colombia’s Cali and Medellín cartels established early footholds in Spanish regions such as Galicia, and Europol issued warnings regarding their resurgence back in 2013. However, current operations reflect an unprecedented degree of sophistication and integration. Europol recently disclosed that among 731 of the most threatening criminal networks identified across the European Union, 149 maintain direct connections to Latin American organisations. Of these networks, 67 incorporate Latin American members, while 22 are predominantly composed of them, directing operations that impact European security, including mobile rings engaged in organised property crime.

While logistical hubs remain entrenched in Spain, Portugal, Belgium, the Netherlands, and France, cartels are rapidly venturing into new territories. According to Daniel Brombacher, director of the Europe Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, syndicates are actively establishing themselves in jurisdictions lacking any prior infrastructure. Recent police raids dismantled Mexican-operated methamphetamine laboratories in southern France, north-eastern Poland, and Brandenburg, Germany. Simultaneously, Latin American factions are surfacing along the Balkan trafficking route traversing Romania and Bulgaria, with activities also documented in Croatia and Slovakia.

The operational footprint may be significantly larger than public records indicate. A confidential report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, incorporating data from the Brazilian intelligence agency Abin, reveals that Brazil’s foremost syndicate, the Primeiro Comando da Capital, operates across sixteen European countries, spanning Ireland, the United Kingdom, Iceland, Sweden, Switzerland, Serbia, and Turkey. Mexican academic Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés observes that major syndicates like the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel have representatives in over twenty European countries. Rather than controlling sprawling local territories, these operatives function primarily as commercial emissaries, orchestrating joint ventures with domestic mafias.

This transcontinental expansion is underpinned by historic manufacturing booms in South America. According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report, global cocaine production surged fourfold over the past decade to an unprecedented volume between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes, while coca cultivation expanded to a record 385,000 hectares. In Colombia, cocaine output now surpasses levels recorded during the infamous era of Pablo Escobar. For these cartels, Europe represents an exceptionally lucrative destination: profit margins are substantially higher than in the United States, and European forces have intercepted more narcotics than their American counterparts since the start of the decade. With Europe now consuming roughly one-quarter of worldwide supplies, foreign syndicates possess powerful financial incentives to permanently entrench their European presence.

facts.fact: A four-month Guardian investigation found that Latin American criminal networks are operating in at least 12 European countries, forging ties with local mafias.
Between 2014 and 2024, European cocaine seizures rose by 471% as local processing laboratories were dismantled.

Identified groups include Mexico's Sinaloa and CJNG cartels, Colombia's Clan del Golfo, ELN, and Farc dissidents, Brazil's PCC and Comando Vermelho, Venezuela's Tren de Aragua, and gangs MS-13 and Barrio 18.

An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor's office indicates that Brazil's PCC operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland, and Turkey.
The UNODC 2026 World Drug Report found global cocaine production reached between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes in 2024, more than four times the 2014 level, with coca cultivation covering 385,000 hectares.

Europol reported that of 731 most threatening criminal networks active across Europe, 149 are linked to Latin American syndicates, with 67 including Latin American members and 22 consisting mostly of them.
Europe now represents roughly a quarter of global cocaine consumption, offering traffickers higher profit margins than the United States.
